\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{graphicx}
\setlist{nosep}
\setlist{topsep=2pt}
\usepackage{enumitem}
\renewcommand{\baselinestrech}{1.15}

\title{Calving Dynamics of a Tidewater Glacier:\\Two Decades of Terminus Observations}
\author{E.~R.~Aaltonen and C.~Vidal}
\date{April 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
We analyse twenty years of terminus positions, ice velocities, and surface
elevation change for a marine-terminating glacier draining into a
subarctic fjord. The record shows three retreat phases separated by two
readvances, each associated with changes in the timing of the melt season
rather than with fjord temperature alone. We argue that the calving front
position is controlled jointly by crevasse-depth calving at the terminus
and by seasonal undercutting at the waterline, and we provide a simple
parameterisation that reproduces the observed migration with a skill of
0.81 in a leave-three-years-out validation.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Tidewater glaciers lose most of their mass by iceberg calving rather than
by surface melt, and the position of the \textb{calving front} is the
single most important geometric control on the calving flux. Understanding
why termini retreat or advance on seasonal to decadal timescales is
therefore central to projecting the contribution of land ice to sea level
rise over the coming century.

Two families of calving models dominate the literature. Crevasse-depth
models relate calving to the penetration of surface and basal crevasses,
which depends on the stretching rate and on the depth of surface
meltwater. Fjord-process models emphasise melting and undercutting at the
ice--ocean interface, which weaken the terminus mechanically and trigger
calving events. Observational tests that can discriminate between the two
families are scarce, because they require simultaneous records of terminus
position, velocity, and fjord conditions over many years.

Here we assemble such a record for a mid-sized tidewater glacier in a
subarctic fjord system. The glacier retreated by 3.1~km over the study
period, but the retreat was not monotonic: two readvances of several
hundred metres interrupted the general trend, and each readvance lasted
between three and five years. We use this behaviour to test the two model
families and to build a hybrid parameterisation.

The glacier is representative of a class of mid-sized outlets whose mass
loss is dominated by dynamics rather than by surface mass balance, and
whose termini rest on shallow sills near the fjord mouth. Because these
glaciers respond to forcing on timescales of years rather than decades,
they offer a natural laboratory for testing calving physics against
observations that resolve individual retreat and readvance events.

\section{Data}
The terminus position is mapped from optical satellite imagery at 16-day
resolution between 2003 and 2023, supplemented by radar imagery during
the polar night. Ice velocity is derived from feature tracking on
overlapping image pairs and validated against stakes measured by
differential positioning in the lower ablation area. Surface elevation
change is taken from repeated airborne laser scanning and from satellite
altimetry, both reduced to a common reference surface.

Fjord hydrography is sampled by two moorings located 2~km and 12~km from
the 2010 terminus position, each carrying temperature and conductivity
sensors at ten depths. Runoff is estimated from a regional climate model
downscaled to 1~km and validated against the gauged catchment of a
neighbouring land-terminating glacier.

\section{Methods}
The stretching rate at the terminus is computed from the velocity
gradient along the flowline, smoothed over 400~m to suppress noise from
individual tracking errors. Crevasse penetration is estimated following
the zero-stress model, in which the surface crevasse depth $d_s$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
d_s = \frac{2}{\rho_i g}\left(\frac{\dot{\epsilon}}{A}\right)^{1/n} + \frac{\rho_w}{\rho_i} d_w,
\end{equation}
where $\dot{\epsilon}$ is the stretching rate, $A$ and $n$ are the flow
law parameters, and $d_w$ is the water depth in the crevasse. Calving is
assumed to occur when the total penetration reaches the full ice thickness.

The undercutting rate is parameterised as a function of the thermal
forcing at the waterline and the subglacial discharge. The melt rate
$\dot{m}$ follows the standard three-equation formulation with transfer
coefficients taken from laboratory constraints, and the undercut is
converted into a calving increment when its horizontal extent exceeds a
critical fraction of the ice thickness.

The hybrid model advances the terminus when the simulated ice flux across
the grounding line exceeds the sum of the two calving contributions, and
retreats it otherwise. Model skill is evaluated with the coefficient of
determination $v^2^*$ in a leave-three-years-out cross-validation over
the full record.

All three tunable coefficients are estimated on the training folds only,
using a bounded search over the literature ranges. The crevasse water
depth is taken proportional to the modelled runoff with a delay of two
weeks, and the critical undercut fraction is uniform across the record.
No parameter is allowed to vary between retreat and readvance phases, so
that the validation tests the physics rather than the fitting.

\section{Results}
The observed terminus migration decomposes into a seasonal cycle of
200--400~m and a decadal trend that dominates the total displacement.
Retreat phases in 2005--2009 and 2016--2021 account for most of the net
loss, while the readvances in 2010--2012 and 2022--2023 temporarily
recovered about one fifth of the lost distance.

Velocity at the terminus varies in phase with the migration: the glacier
accelerates by about 30 percent during retreat phases and decelerates
during readvances, with a lag of roughly one melt season between the
velocity signal and the terminus response. Surface lowering over the
lower ablation area reached 45~m over the full record, and the lowering
propagated up-glacier at a rate consistent with diffusive thinning.

Three findings emerge from the comparison with the model families:
\begin{itemize}
\item crevasse-depth calving reproduces the seasonal cycle but fails to
produce the multi-year readvances;
\item fjord-process calving reproduces the decadal trend but not the
timing of the spring retreat onset;
\item the hybrid model reproduces both the seasonal cycle and the
readvances, with a cross-validated skill of 0.81.
\end{itemize}

\section{Discussion}
The readvances coincide with two periods of reduced summer runoff rather
than with anomalous fjord temperatures, which suggests that subglacial
discharge modulates the undercutting strongly enough to reverse the sign
of the terminus migration for several years at a time. This mechanism is
absent from crevasse-depth models and is only partly captured by
fjord-process models that neglect the discharge dependence of the melt
rate.

The parameterisation developed here is deliberately simple: it has three
tunable coefficients, all constrained within their literature ranges, and
it can be implemented in an ice-sheet model at negligible cost. Its main
limitation is the assumption of a well-mixed fjord, which is violated
during the spring freshet, when the plume structure is strongly
stratified and the transfer coefficients are likely to vary in time.

A second limitation is that the record, although long by the standards of
tidewater studies, contains only two complete readvance events, so the
readvance branch of the parameterisation is constrained by a small sample.
Extending the analysis to the neighbouring outlets of the fjord system,
which share the same ocean forcing but differ in geometry, is the most
direct way to test whether the fitted coefficients transfer across
glaciers or must be retuned for each terminus.

The main data products used in this study are:
\begin{itemize}
\item terminus positions at 16-day resolution over 2003--2023;
\item flowline velocities from feature tracking and ground stakes;
\item elevation change from airborne scanning and satellite altimetry;
\item terminus position from repeat imagery.
\section{Conclusion}
Two decades of observations show that the terminus of a mid-sized
tidewater glacier is shaped jointly by crevasse penetration and by
discharge-modulated undercutting. A hybrid parameterisation that combines
the two mechanisms reproduces the observed migration with high skill and
offers a tractable way to represent calving in regional ice-sheet models.
Future work will test the parameterisation on the remaining outlet
glaciers of the fjord system, with particular attention to glaciers whose
termini are currently advancing.
\end{document}
